paragraphs: Mitya spoke sullenly, but it was clear he was trying harder than ever not to forget or skip a single detail. He told them how he had jumped over the fence into his father’s garden and gone up to the window. He told them everything that happened under that window. He described, clearly, precisely, point by point, the feelings that tormented him in the garden, when he was desperate to know whether Grushenka was with his father or not. But, strange to say, both lawyers now listened with a kind of chilling reserve. They looked at him coldly and asked few questions. Mitya could read nothing from their faces.
“They’re angry and offended,” he thought. “Well, to hell with them!”

He described how he finally decided to give his father the “signal” that Grushenka had come, so that the old man would open the window. The lawyers paid no attention to the word “signal.” They seemed not to grasp what it meant in this context, so plainly that Mitya noticed. Then he came to the moment when he saw his father peering out of the window, felt his hatred flare up and pulled the pestle out of his pocket. Suddenly, as if on purpose, he stopped short. He sat staring at the wall, aware that their eyes were fixed on him.
“Well?” said the investigating lawyer. “You pulled out the weapon and ... and what happened then?”
“Then? Why, then I murdered him ... hit him on the head and split his skull.... I suppose that’s your story. That’s it!”
His eyes suddenly flashed. All the anger he had smothered flared up in his soul with extraordinary violence.
“Our story?” repeated Nikolay Parfenovitch. “Well, and yours?”
Mitya dropped his eyes and was silent for a long time.

“My story, gentlemen? Well, it was like this,” he began softly. “Maybe it was someone’s tears, or my mother praying to God, or a good angel kissing me at that moment. I don’t know. But the devil was beaten. I rushed away from the window and ran to the fence. My father was alarmed. For the first time he saw me, and he cried out and jumped back from the window. I remember that very well. I ran across the garden to the fence ... and there Grigory caught me, as I was sitting on the fence.”
At that point he finally raised his eyes and looked at his listeners. They seemed to be staring at him with perfectly calm attention. A kind of fit of indignation seized Mitya’s soul.
“Why, you’re laughing at me right now, gentlemen!” he broke off suddenly.
“What makes you think that?” observed Nikolay Parfenovitch.

“You don’t believe a word of it, that’s why! Of course I understand that I’ve come to the vital point. The old man is lying there now with his skull broken, while I—after telling you so dramatically how I wanted to kill him and how I snatched up the pestle—suddenly run away from the window. A romance! Poetry! As if anyone could take a fellow’s word for it. Ha ha! You’re scoffers, gentlemen!”
And he swung round on his chair so hard that it creaked.
“And did you notice,” the prosecutor asked suddenly, as though he had not seen Mitya’s agitation, “when you ran away from the window, whether the door into the garden was open?”
“No, it wasn’t open.”
“It wasn’t?”
“It was shut. And who could have opened it? Bah! The door. Wait a minute!” he seemed suddenly to remember something, and almost with a start he went on:
“Why, did you find the door open?”
“Yes, it was open.”
“Why, who could have opened it, if you didn’t open it yourselves?” cried Mitya, astonished.

“The door stood open. Your father’s murderer undoubtedly went in by that door, and after committing the crime he went out again by the same door,” the prosecutor said slowly, as though chiseling out each word separately. “That is perfectly clear. The murder was committed in the room and _not through the window_. That is absolutely certain from the examination that has been made, from the position of the body and everything else. There can be no doubt about it.”
Mitya was completely dumbfounded.

“But that’s utterly impossible!” he cried, totally at a loss. “I ... I didn’t go in.... I tell you positively, definitely, the door was shut the whole time I was in the garden, and when I ran out of the garden. I only stood at the window and saw him through the window. That’s all, that’s all.... I remember it to the last minute. And even if I didn’t remember, it would make no difference. I know it, because nobody knew the signals except Smerdyakov, me and the dead man. And he wouldn’t have opened the door to anyone in the world without the signals.”

“Signals? What signals?” asked the prosecutor, with greedy, almost hysterical curiosity. He instantly lost every trace of his reserve and dignity. He asked the question with a sort of cringing timidity. He had scented an important fact he had known nothing about, and he was already afraid that Mitya might refuse to reveal it.

“So you didn’t know!” Mitya winked at him with a malicious, mocking smile. “What if I won’t tell you? Who else could you find out from? No one knew about the signals except my father, Smerdyakov and me. That’s all. Heaven knew, too, but Heaven won’t tell you. But it’s an interesting fact. There’s no telling what you might build on it. Ha ha! Take comfort, gentlemen, I’ll reveal it. You’ve got some foolish idea in your heads. You don’t know the man you’re dealing with! You’re dealing with a prisoner who gives evidence against himself, to his own harm! Yes, because I’m a man of honor and you—are not.”

The prosecutor swallowed this without a murmur. He was trembling with impatience to hear the new fact. Mitya told them everything about the signals that Fyodor Pavlovitch had invented for Smerdyakov, minutely and at great length. He told them exactly what each tap on the window meant. He tapped the signals out on the table. When Nikolay Parfenovitch said that he supposed Mitya had tapped the signal “Grushenka has come” when he tapped on his father’s window, Mitya answered precisely that yes, he had tapped that signal, that “Grushenka had come.”
“So now you can build your tower,” Mitya broke off, and again turned away from them with contempt.
“So no one knew of the signals except your dead father, you, and the valet Smerdyakov? And no one else?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked once more.
“Yes. The valet Smerdyakov, and Heaven. Write down about Heaven. That may be of use. Besides, you’ll need God yourselves.”
And they had already, of course, begun writing it down. But while they wrote, the prosecutor said suddenly, as though pouncing on a new idea:

“But if Smerdyakov also knew of these signals, and you absolutely deny any responsibility for your father’s death, was it not perhaps he who knocked the agreed signal, got your father to open the door to him, and then ... committed the crime?”
Mitya turned on him a look of deep irony and intense hatred. His silent stare lasted so long that the prosecutor blinked.

“You’ve caught the fox again,” Mitya said at last. “You’ve got the beast by the tail. Ha ha! I see through you, Mr. Prosecutor. You thought, of course, that I’d jump at that, seize on your suggestion, and shout with all my might, ‘Aie! It’s Smerdyakov! He’s the murderer!’ Admit it, that’s what you thought. Admit it, and I’ll go on.”
But the prosecutor did not admit it. He held his tongue and waited.
“You’re mistaken. I’m not going to shout ‘It’s Smerdyakov,’” said Mitya.
“And you don’t even suspect him?”
“Why, do you suspect him?”
“He is suspected, too.”
Mitya fixed his eyes on the floor.

“Joking aside,” he brought out gloomily. “Listen. From the very beginning, almost from the moment I ran out to you from behind the curtain, I’ve had the thought of Smerdyakov in my mind. I’ve been sitting here shouting that I’m innocent and thinking all the time, ‘Smerdyakov!’ I can’t get Smerdyakov out of my head. In fact, I thought of Smerdyakov just now, too, but only for a second. Almost at once I thought, ‘No, it’s not Smerdyakov.’ It’s not his doing, gentlemen.”
“In that case, is there anyone else you suspect?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked cautiously.
“I don’t know who it could be, whether it’s the hand of Heaven or of Satan, but ... not Smerdyakov,” Mitya jerked out decisively.
“But what makes you so confident and so emphatic that it’s not he?”

“From my conviction—my impression. Because Smerdyakov is a man of the most abject character, and a coward. He’s not just a coward, he’s all the cowardice in the world walking on two legs. He has the heart of a chicken. When he talked to me, he was always trembling for fear I would kill him, though I never raised a hand against him. He fell at my feet and blubbered. He has kissed these very boots, literally, begging me ‘not to frighten him.’ Do you hear? ‘Not to frighten him.’ What a thing to say! Why, I offered him money. He’s a whining chicken—sickly, epileptic, weak-minded—a child of eight could thrash him. He has no character worth talking about. It’s not Smerdyakov, gentlemen. He doesn’t care for money; he wouldn’t take my presents. Besides, what motive would he have for murdering the old man? Why, he’s very likely his son, you know—his natural son. Do you know that?”
“We have heard that story. But you are your father’s son, too, you know, and yet you yourself told everyone you meant to murder him.”

“That’s a thrust! And a nasty, mean one, too! I’m not afraid! Oh, gentlemen, isn’t it too base of you to say that to my face? It’s base, because I told you that myself. I not only wanted to murder him, I might have done it. And what’s more, I went out of my way to tell you, of my own accord, that I nearly murdered him. But you see, I didn’t murder him. You see, my guardian angel saved me—that’s what you haven’t taken into account. And that’s why it’s so base of you. Because I didn’t kill him, I didn’t kill him! Do you hear? I did not kill him.”
He was almost choking. He had not been so moved at any point in the whole interrogation.
“And what has he told you, gentlemen—Smerdyakov, I mean?” he added suddenly, after a pause. “May I ask that question?”

“You may ask any question,” the prosecutor replied with icy severity, “any question relating to the facts of the case, and we are, I repeat, bound to answer every inquiry you make. We found the servant Smerdyakov, whom you ask about, lying unconscious in his bed, in an epileptic fit of extreme severity, which had recurred, possibly, ten times. The doctor who was with us told us, after examining him, that he may not live through the night.”
“Well, if that’s so, the devil must have killed him,” broke suddenly from Mitya, as though until that moment he had been asking himself: “Was it Smerdyakov or not?”
“We will come back to this later,” Nikolay Parfenovitch decided. “Now, wouldn’t you like to continue your statement?”

Mitya asked for a rest, and his request was courteously granted. After resting, he went on with his story. But he was clearly depressed. He was exhausted, humiliated and shaken to the core. To make things worse, the prosecutor irritated him, as though on purpose, with annoying interruptions about “trifling points.” Mitya had barely described how, sitting on the wall, he had struck Grigory on the head with the pestle while the old man held on to his left leg, and how he had then jumped down to look at him, when the prosecutor stopped him and asked him to describe exactly how he had been sitting on the wall. Mitya was surprised.
“Oh, I was sitting like this, astride, one leg on one side of the wall and one on the other.”
“And the pestle?”
“The pestle was in my hand.”
“Not in your pocket? Do you remember that precisely? Was it a violent blow you gave him?”
“It must have been a violent one. But why do you ask?”
“Would you mind sitting on the chair just as you sat on the wall then, and showing us exactly how you moved your arm, and in what direction?”
“You’re making fun of me, aren’t you?” asked Mitya, looking haughtily at the speaker. But the man did not flinch.
Mitya turned abruptly, sat astride his chair and swung his arm.
“This is how I struck him! That’s how I knocked him down! What more do you want?”
“Thank you. May I trouble you now to explain why you jumped down, what your purpose was, and what you had in view?”
